title: The shadow behind the core
teaches: How missing waves on the far side of the Earth revealed the core, and how S waves showed it is liquid

parts.title: Late waves from the far side

blocks.text: Lesson D1 ended with a dense core proposed from the Earth's weight. Seismographs offered a way to look for it directly. In 1906 Richard Dixon Oldham, a geologist with the Geological Survey of India who had studied the great Assam earthquake of 1897, gathered records of distant earthquakes and plotted how long their P waves and S waves took to arrive against the distance travelled. Out to about a third of the way round the Earth, the points fell on smooth curves: the farther the station, the longer the trip, in a steady way. Waves that had to cross the middle of the Earth, to stations near the opposite side, arrived noticeably later than those curves predicted, especially the waves he took to be S waves, as if something in the centre slowed them.

Oldham's data were sparse, and the late arrivals he took to be S waves on the far side were actually reflected waves of other kinds. But his conclusion was right: the Earth has a central core in which earthquake waves travel more slowly than in the rock around it.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Oldham (1906) found that waves crossing the centre of the Earth arrived late.
He proposed a central core where waves travel more slowly.

blocks.text: To see what a slow core does, follow a wave through the Earth. Distances around the Earth are given as angles measured from the Earth's centre: a station 90° from a quake is a quarter of the way around, 180° is directly opposite. The speed of a wave in rock depends on how stiff the rock is compared with how dense: stiffer rock springs back faster and passes the wave on faster. In the mantle, the weight of the rock above squeezes it, and it gets stiffer with depth faster than it gets denser, so P waves speed up from about 8 kilometres a second at the top of the mantle to about 13.7 at its base. A wave heading down at a slant runs into ever faster rock, and like a car with its outer wheels on a faster surface it is turned gradually back toward the surface, coming up again some distance away. The closer to straight down it starts, the deeper it goes and the farther away it comes up. (The Earth's radius is 6,371 kilometres, for scale.)

Now add a core where waves travel more slowly, about 8 kilometres a second at its top against 13.7 just above it. A wave crossing into slower material is turned to a path closer to straight down, toward the centre, as light is when it passes from air into water; a wave crossing into faster material is turned the other way, toward a flatter path. Waves that only just miss the core travel on through the mantle and come up about 100° away; a little energy bends round the core's edge and reaches a few degrees farther, so the edge is usually quoted as about 104°. Waves that only just hit the core are turned sharply inward, cross it, and are turned again as they leave, coming up much farther around the Earth, beyond about 140°. Between those distances no direct P wave arrives at all: there is a **shadow zone**.

blocks.caption: Wave paths from an earthquake at the top, through half of the Earth, drawn to scale; distances round the surface are angles from the centre. Every sixth path of many is drawn. The mantle's speeds follow measured values (8 km/s at the top to 13.7 at the base), simplified; you set the core. In this simple model the shadow starts at about 100°.

blocks.text: In 1914 Beno Gutenberg, then at Göttingen in Germany and later at Caltech, used many more records to map the shadow: direct P waves fade beyond about 104° from a quake and reappear at about 142°. From the edges of the shadow he calculated the depth of the core's surface: 2,900 kilometres, a little under halfway to the centre. The modern figure is 2,890. The core's radius is 3,480 kilometres, just over half the Earth's 6,371, which is the size of core that lesson D1's density and moment of inertia called for.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Waves speed up with depth in the mantle and curve back to the surface.
Waves entering the slower core are bent inward, leaving a shadow zone where no direct P waves arrive, from about 104° to 140°.
Gutenberg (1914) put the top of the core at 2,900 km depth; the modern value is 2,890 km.

blocks.text: S waves told a more extreme story. They arrive at stations up to about 104°, the same edge as the P shadow, because the same core boundary sets it. Beyond that no direct S waves arrive at all, anywhere on the far side of the Earth. Lesson D2 explained why that would be: S waves cannot travel through liquid.

In 1926 the British geophysicist Harold Jeffreys settled the question by combining earthquake waves with the tides. The Moon's and Sun's gravity raise tides in the solid Earth as well as in the oceans: the ground itself rises and falls by about 30 centimetres twice a day. How much it does so depends on how stiff the Earth is overall. The mantle's stiffness was known from its S-wave speeds, and Jeffreys showed that if the core were as stiff as the mantle, the Earth as a whole would be stiffer and would flex less than the tides show it does. The core had to be far less rigid than the mantle, and together with the missing S waves the simplest answer was that it is liquid. (Lesson D5 shows that its very centre is different; the liquid part is now called the **outer core**.) Molten iron, kept liquid by the heat inside the Earth, fits the density, the shadow and the tides.
Use the switch in the figure to send S waves instead of P. Every S wave that reaches the core stops there, and the S shadow covers the whole far side of the Earth.

blocks.caption: The Earth's layers to scale, with the depths of their boundaries.

blocks.text: A liquid iron core also explains something the course met in lesson 9. The Earth's magnetic field cannot come from a giant bar magnet inside, because iron loses its permanent magnetism above about 770 °C and the core is thousands of degrees hotter. Instead, heat and buoyant light elements escaping from the inner core keep the liquid iron slowly churning, and iron conducts electricity: a conductor moving through a magnetic field generates electric currents, and those currents make a magnetic field of their own, which keeps the process going, as in a dynamo. Because it depends on the flow, the field can weaken and reverse, which is what left the stripes on the sea floor.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: No direct S waves arrive beyond about 104°, because they cannot cross the core.
Jeffreys (1926) showed from the Earth's tides and mantle wave speeds that the core has negligible rigidity; with the missing S waves, that means it is liquid.
Churning molten iron in the outer core, acting as a dynamo, generates the Earth's magnetic field.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the core
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why do waves heading down into the mantle curve back up to the surface?
choices: Waves travel faster with depth in the mantle, which bends them back upward
They bounce off the bottom of the crust
The Earth's gravity pulls them back up
items.why: A wave running into faster rock is turned toward a flatter path, so a wave going down at a slant gradually turns back toward the surface.

items.ask: What causes the P-wave shadow zone?
choices: Waves entering the slower core are bent sharply inward, so none arrive directly between about 104° and 140°
The core absorbs all P waves
The shadow zone is where the oceans are
items.why: Waves that just miss the core come up before about 104°. Those that just hit it are turned inward by the slower core, so they cross it and come up beyond about 140°. No path lands in between.

items.ask: Why does no direct S wave reach the far side of the Earth?
choices: The outer core is liquid, and S waves cannot pass through liquid
S waves are too slow to cross the Earth before fading
S waves are reflected by the Moho
items.why: S waves need a material that springs back when sheared. Liquid iron does not, so S waves stop at the core.

items.ask: How did Jeffreys use the tides to show the core is liquid?
choices: The solid Earth flexes more under tides than it would if the core were rigid
Ocean tides are higher above the core
The tides make the core spin faster
items.why: The Earth's overall stiffness, measured from its tidal flexing, was too low for a rigid core.

items.ask: How far down is the top of the core?
items.why: Gutenberg calculated 2,900 km from the edges of the shadow zone in 1914. The modern value is 2,890 km.

learned: Oldham (1906) found waves crossing the Earth's centre arrived late; Gutenberg (1914) mapped the P shadow zone and put the core's top at 2,900 km.
Waves bend inward entering the slower core, which leaves a shadow from about 104° to 140°.
S waves stop at the core, and Jeffreys (1926) showed from tides that it is liquid; its churning makes the magnetic field.
